label: Unit roots, differencing and ARIMA — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The process yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + εₜ is:
items.explanation: It is the AR(1) with φ = 1 exactly. Unrolling gives yₜ as the sum of all shocks to date, so Var(yₜ) = tσ²ε grows without limit and stationarity fails. It is the simplest unit-root process, ARIMA(0, 1, 0).

items.stem: For the random walk with drift yₜ = μ + yₜ₋₁ + εₜ starting from y₀ = 0, the mean and variance of yₜ are:
items.explanation: Unrolling gives yₜ = μt + (ε₁ + … + εₜ), so the drift accumulates into a mean of μt and the uncorrelated shocks accumulate into a variance of tσ²ε. Both depend on t, so neither the constant-mean nor the constant-variance requirement of stationarity holds.
items.check: Both quantities must carry a factor of t, because both the drift and the shocks accumulate. An answer where either is free of t has not unrolled the recursion.

items.stem: If φ₁ + φ₂ = 1 in an AR(2) process, the process:
items.explanation: φ(1) = 1 − φ₁ − φ₂ = 0, so z = 1 is a root of the AR polynomial and (1 − B) factors out. The process is not stationary. Its variance is finite at each finite t but grows without bound, and its correlation depends on both t and lag, so there is no time-invariant ACF depending only on lag. Difference it before applying stationary ACF-based identification methods.

items.stem: An ARIMA(2, 1, 0) process becomes stationary after:
items.explanation: The middle number of ARIMA(p, d, q) is d, the number of differencings required — here 1. The 2 is the AR order of what remains, so after one differencing the series is a stationary AR(2). Confusing p with d is the standard error.
items.check: Read the middle number. It is d, not the AR order and not the MA order.

items.stem: The MA(1) process yₜ = εₜ − θεₜ₋₁ is invertible if:
items.explanation: The MA polynomial is 1 − θz, whose root 1/θ lies outside the unit circle exactly when |θ| < 1. This is the same condition on θ that stationarity imposes on φ for an AR(1) — the invertibility region mirrors the stationarity region.

items.stem: The Dickey–Fuller test is used to test for:
items.explanation: It tests whether a series has a unit root, and the unit root is its NULL hypothesis — so failing to reject points towards differencing the series. The alternative is stationarity.

items.stem: A sample ACF that decays very slowly and almost linearly, and is still large at lag 20, suggests:
options: a unit root — difference the series
items.explanation: A stationary AR or MA ACF decays geometrically and would be negligible by lag 20. A random walk's ACF is √(t/(t+k)), which at t = 100 is still 0.913 at lag 20 and 0.816 at lag 50 — exactly this slow, near-linear pattern. The remedy is differencing, confirmed formally by a Dickey–Fuller test.

items.stem: For yₜ = 1.2yₜ₋₁ − 0.2yₜ₋₂ + εₜ, the differenced series Δyₜ is:
items.explanation: The coefficients sum to 1.2 − 0.2 = 1, so there is a unit root. Factoring: 1 − 1.2B + 0.2B² = (1 − B)(1 − 0.2B), so (1 − 0.2B)Δyₜ = εₜ and therefore Δyₜ = +0.2Δyₜ₋₁ + εₜ. The sign comes from the factor (1 − 0.2B); reading −0.2 off the original equation gives the wrong answer.

items.stem: For a random walk with y₀ = 0 observed at t = 100, the correlation between y₁₀₀ and y₁₁₀ is:
items.explanation: Corr(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) = √(t/(t + k)) = √(100/110) = 0.953. The first option is the lag-1 value √(100/101) and the third is the lag-20 value √(100/120). The point is how slowly this falls: a stationary AR(1) with φ = 0.9 would already be at 0.9¹⁰ = 0.35 by lag 10.
items.check: The correlation depends on both t and k — which is itself proof of non-stationarity, since a stationary ACF depends on k alone.

items.stem: For a process with φ₁ = 0.4, φ₂ = 0.3, θ₁ = 0.6, θ₂ = 0.4 (MA written with minus signs), the process is:
items.explanation: Stationarity uses the φ triangle: 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7 < 1 ✓, 0.3 − 0.4 = −0.1 < 1 ✓, |0.3| < 1 ✓ — stationary. Invertibility uses the same triangle on the θ values: 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.0, which is not less than 1 ✗. The MA part sits exactly on the boundary, an MA unit root, so the process is not invertible.

items.stem: Which statement about a finite moving-average process is correct?
options: it is always stationary, whatever its coefficients
its stationarity depends on the sample size
items.explanation: A finite MA is a weighted sum of finitely many shocks, so its variance is finite and its autocovariances depend only on the lag — stationarity is automatic. The |θ| < 1 condition is for INVERTIBILITY, not stationarity, and conflating the two is the trap this question sets.

items.stem: Consider a series with a unit root.
items.explanation: A is true — the variance of a random walk is tσ²ε, finite for each finite t but unbounded as t grows. B is true in the stationary-ACF sense: the correlation is still defined at each t and lag, but it is not a function of lag alone. C is false — a unit root is the boundary case, and roots inside the unit circle give explosive behaviour. D is true, and it is the practical hazard the regression literature is built around.
statements: The variance grows without limit as t increases.
There is no time-invariant autocorrelation function depending only on lag.
The process is explosive, with values growing geometrically.
Regressing one such series on another can produce a spurious relationship.

A.why: True. For a random walk Var(yₜ) = tσ²ε, which grows linearly in t and has no limit.

B.why: True in the stationary-ACF sense. The time-specific correlation exists, but depends on both t and k; there is no lag-only ACF because the variance is not constant.

C.why: False. A unit root sits exactly ON the unit circle and gives a wandering, not an exploding, series. Explosive behaviour needs a root strictly inside the circle, equivalently coefficients summing to more than 1.

D.why: True. Two independent random walks that both happen to drift produce a strong apparent relationship, and the problem worsens as the sample grows.

items.stem: In the Dickey–Fuller regression Δyₜ = δyₜ₋₁ + εₜ, the hypotheses are:
items.explanation: Starting from yₜ = φyₜ₋₁ + εₜ and subtracting yₜ₋₁ gives δ = φ − 1. A unit root means φ = 1, so δ = 0 — the null. Stationarity means φ < 1, so δ < 0, and the alternative is one-sided in the negative direction.

items.stem: A Dickey–Fuller test returns a p-value of 0.31. The correct action is:
options: conclude the series is stationary and model it directly
treat the series as non-stationary and difference it
conclude a unit root has been proved
items.explanation: The null is the unit root, so a large p-value means insufficient evidence against non-stationarity, and the appropriate action is to difference. It does not PROVE a unit root — the test has low power against a φ near 1 — but differencing is the conservative and conventional response.

items.stem: Over-differencing a series that was already stationary:
options: introduces a unit root into the MA part
items.explanation: Differencing a stationary series multiplies its model by (1 − B), which puts a unit root in the MA part — detectable as artificially strong negative autocorrelation at lag 1 and an inflated variance. It is why the rule is to difference as few times as makes the series stationary and no more.

items.stem: For the process yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + εₜ − 0.4εₜ₋₁, the classification and ARIMA order are:
items.explanation: The AR coefficient is exactly 1, a unit root, so the process is not stationary whatever the MA part does. The MA part has |−0.4| < 1 so it is invertible. No AR terms remain after differencing, one difference, one MA term: ARIMA(0, 1, 1), and Δyₜ = εₜ − 0.4εₜ₋₁ is a stationary invertible MA(1).
items.check: Check the AR part first; a unit root there settles non-stationarity. Then count: p = 0, d = 1, q = 1.

items.stem: Consider the Dickey–Fuller test and its critical values.
items.explanation: A is true and is the reason the standard theory fails. B is true — the critical values are around −2.9 at 5% with a constant, against about −1.65 from the t distribution. C is false: using the t table makes the test reject too EASILY, declaring stationarity that is not supported. D is true, and it is why the two tests are often run together.
statements: Under the null the regressor yₜ₋₁ is non-stationary, so the usual asymptotic theory does not apply.
The correct critical values are more negative than the ordinary t values.
Using an ordinary t table makes the test too conservative.
The KPSS test reverses the hypotheses, taking stationarity as its null.

A.why: True. Σyₜ₋₁² grows like n² rather than n under the null, so the limit is not normal — it involves integrals of Brownian motion and was tabulated by simulation.

B.why: True — about −2.9 at the 5% level with a constant, against roughly −1.65 from the t distribution.

C.why: False, and the direction matters. More negative correct values mean the t table rejects too readily, so the error is declaring stationarity that the data do not support — the more damaging direction.

D.why: True. KPSS takes stationarity as its null, so the two are often run together; agreement is reassuring and disagreement shows the data cannot settle the question.

items.stem: Two AR(2) processes both have a unit root: yₜ = 0.6yₜ₋₁ + 0.4yₜ₋₂ + εₜ and yₜ = 1.2yₜ₋₁ − 0.2yₜ₋₂ + εₜ. Their differenced series are:
options: AR(1) with φ = −0.4 and AR(1) with φ = 0.2
AR(1) with φ = 0.6 and AR(1) with φ = 1.2
items.explanation: The polynomials factor as (1 − B)(1 + 0.4B) and (1 − B)(1 − 0.2B) respectively, so the differenced series satisfy Δyₜ = −0.4Δyₜ₋₁ + εₜ and Δyₜ = +0.2Δyₜ₋₁ + εₜ. Both are ARIMA(1, 1, 0) and the surviving coefficients have opposite signs — the sign comes from the factorisation, never from the original equation, which is what the third option wrongly assumes.

items.stem: Why is an invertible canonical representation imposed when fitting a moving-average model, given that a finite MA is always stationary?
options: because without it the variance is infinite
because the ACF would not decay
because the mean would depend on time
because the shocks cannot otherwise be recovered from the data, and two parameter values give the same ACF
items.explanation: An MA(1) with coefficient θ and one with 1/θ have the same autocorrelation function. Matching the full autocovariance structure also requires rescaling the innovation variance. Invertibility selects the canonical member of this observationally equivalent pair and makes its innovations recoverable through a convergent inverse filter. A non-invertible parameterisation's original shocks are not recoverable through that inverse, but the observed process has an equivalent invertible representation for forecasting.

items.stem: An analyst reads p and q from the sample ACF and PACF of an undifferenced series that has a unit root. The result is:
options: uninformative, because the slow decay of a non-stationary ACF swamps any AR or MA pattern
valid, since the ACF and PACF are computed the same way regardless
valid only if the series has drift
items.explanation: A unit-root series has an ACF near 1 at every short lag and decaying almost linearly, so it carries no usable information about order — it would suggest a very high AR order at every attempt. This is why d must be determined FIRST, and why a question describing a slowly decaying ACF is asking about differencing rather than about model order.
